Source: the Quebec MRNF geocoder

Source: vignettes/source-qc.Rmd
source-qc.Rmd

Quebec’s Ministère des Ressources naturelles et des Forêts runs an Esri GeocodeServer over the Répertoire québécois des adresses — the same register rqa_import() loads offline, served live. Two locators sit behind it: RQA_Adresse for addresses and RQA_Rue for streets.

qc_geocode() is the client, "qc" is a geocode() tier, qc_validate() re-asks it about an answer you already have, and qc_reverse_geocode() is the only online reverse geocoder in this package — the other three services do forward only.

library(cangeocode)
library(dplyr)

con <- nar_connection()

What this adds to the package

Reverse geocoding that is not NAR, and a Quebec fallback that needs no import.

The reverse endpoint is the distinctive one. Everything else here answers “where is this address”; qc_reverse_geocode() answers “what address is at this point” against a provincial register, where reverse_geocode() answers it against NAR. In Quebec those are close to the same question — see the warning below — but the service will name an address NAR does not carry.

As a forward fallback it is worth about what NRCan’s geolocator is: on 600 Quebec corporations addresses it takes coverage from 81.0% to 83.3%, recovering 12.3% of what NAR left unplaced. If you have run rqa_import(), the offline "rqa" tier does more than this and does it without the network — see vignette("source-rqa"). The online tier is what you reach for when you have not.

Licence

The register is CC-BY 4.0, the same terms rqa_import() carries, and rqa_attribution() is the string that discharges it:

rqa_attribution()
#> [1] "Contains information licensed under CC-BY 4.0 from the Repertoire quebecois des adresses, Ministere des Ressources naturelles et des Forets, Gouvernement du Quebec."

That composes with the Open Government Licence covering NAR, which is why this can be a default tier where osm_geocode()’s ODbL data cannot.

Using it 

qc_geocode("1 Rue Notre-Dame Ouest, Montreal, QC") |>
  select(match_method, uncertainty_m, qc_locator, qc_score, qc_address, lon, lat)
#>   match_method uncertainty_m  qc_locator qc_score                              qc_address       lon
#> 1   qc_address            20 RQA_Adresse    82.51 1 Rue Notre-Dame Ouest, Montréal H2Y1S5 -73.55596
#>        lat
#> 1 45.50617

Reverse:

qc_reverse_geocode(-73.5555, 45.5019)
#>                                 qc_address qc_postal  qc_city qc_dist_m       lon     lat
#> 1 12-285 Place D'Youville, Montréal H2Y2A4    H2Y2A4 Montréal  11.71217 -73.55552 45.5018

And as a validator against an answer you already have:

g <- geocode(c("1 Rue Notre-Dame Ouest, Montreal, QC",
               "455 Rue Sainte-Catherine Est, Montreal, QC",
               "1020 Rue Bleury, Montreal, QC",
               "2 Cote du Palais, Quebec, QC",
               "150 Boulevard Rene-Levesque Est, Quebec, QC"),
             method = c("nar", "nar_interpolate"), con = con)

qc_validate(g) |>
  select(input, match_method, qc_match_method, qc_score, qc_address, qc_dist_m)
#>                                         input match_method qc_match_method qc_score
#> 1        1 Rue Notre-Dame Ouest, Montreal, QC nar_building      qc_address    82.51
#> 2  455 Rue Sainte-Catherine Est, Montreal, QC nar_building            none    94.12
#> 3               1020 Rue Bleury, Montreal, QC nar_building            none    80.48
#> 4                2 Cote du Palais, Quebec, QC         none            none    94.29
#> 5 150 Boulevard Rene-Levesque Est, Quebec, QC nar_building      qc_address    83.88
#>                                       qc_address qc_dist_m
#> 1        1 Rue Notre-Dame Ouest, Montréal H2Y1S5 0.9305597
#> 2             Rue Sainte-Catherine Est, Montréal        NA
#> 3            1020 Rue De Bleury, Montréal H2Z0B9        NA
#> 4                         Côte du Palais, Québec        NA
#> 5 150 Boulevard René-Lévesque Est, Québec G1R2B2 1.0469956

Two of the five come back with a usable second reading, and the other three are worth walking through, because between them they demonstrate almost everything in the next section. Rows 2 and 4 got street centroids — note the answer has no civic number in it — and row 3 got Rue De Bleury where Rue Bleury was asked for, which is the same street under the name the register prefers. All three were thrown out by the floor rather than by the service, which reported no problem at all; the third is the floor being stricter than it needs to be, which is the side to err on when the alternative is silently accepting a wrong street.

And look at the scores. The two rejected street centroids scored 94.12 and 94.29; the two accepted civic points scored 82.51 and 83.88. The score is not a ranking, and this is what that looks like.

What to watch out for

It is not independent of NAR, so it is a fallback and not a check

The locators are named RQA_Adresse and RQA_Rue. They serve the Répertoire — which is also what NAR’s Quebec records are built from. Over 400 NAR Quebec building points the median disagreement is 0.9 m, p90 13.3 m, nothing over 500 metres; at scale, 2.5 million paired addresses agree to a median of 21 cm.

Those numbers look like a spectacular validation and are nothing of the kind. They are evidence of shared lineage. qc_validate() says so in its own documentation, and the small qc_dist_m in the example above is that effect, not a confirmation. There is no second opinion available for Quebec inside this package — British Columbia is the only province where one exists.

The query has to be spelled French-canonical

This is the reason the tier is worth having at all, and it is not cosmetic. The locator’s reference strings are Rue Notre-Dame Ouest — type first, direction spelled out. NAR’s own canonical form is NOTRE-DAME RUE O. Sent that, the service does not degrade gracefully; it stops matching. On 400 Quebec addresses, by share resolved to a civic point:

rendering civic street only unmatched
NOTRE-DAME RUE O — NAR’s canonical form 31.5% 4.0% 64.5%
NAR order, direction spelled out 58.0% 3.0% 39.0%
French order, direction spelled out 58.8% 14.2% 27.0%
NAR order, type and direction spelled out 95.0% 3.5% 1.5%
French order, type and direction — what the package sends 95.5% 3.5% 1.0%

The abbreviations are what break it; the word order barely matters. Spelling out the direction is worth 26 points, the street type another 37, the order under one.

The failure mode is the worst available: 1 RUE NOTRE-DAME O, MONTREAL comes back as a street centroid scoring 92.4, where the correct civic point scores 82.5. The abbreviated form does not lose the address — it replaces it with a confident wrong answer several hundred metres away. qc_geocode() re-renders every query for you, so you never send the NAR form by accident.

Score is not a precision ranking

Correlation between the score and how far the answer landed from NAR’s building point is Spearman 0.018 — none. Worse, street-only answers score higher than civic ones: civic matches run 75.9–86.2 with a median of 83.0, street centroids 75.8–95.2 with a median of 87.0. The score measures how much of the string you sent was consumed, which a short street name consumes more completely than a long address.

So min_score defaults to 0 here and should stay there. A threshold removes correct addresses before it removes street centroids — the opposite of what min_score does for the BC geocoder.

Loc_name is the precision field. RQA_Adresse is an address, RQA_Rue is a street, and match_method reports that as qc_address or qc_street. Addr_type is Feature for both and separates nothing.

uncertainty_m here is not measured

20 m for qc_address, 500 m for qc_street. Like the BC tiers’ figures, these are precision semantics turned into deliberately pessimistic order-of-magnitude numbers, not error bars comparable to the NAR tiers’.

The floor re-parses the answer, without the gazetteer

The service always returns something, so the package compares the returned title against what was asked for, component by component. That re-parse deliberately runs without the gazetteer — a gazetteer would resolve the returned string back toward the query and launder the very error the check exists to catch.

It earns its keep. 12 RUE SAINT-JEAN, GATINEAU comes back as 12 Rue Saint-Jean-Bosco, Gatineau under RQA_Adresse: right municipality, right civic number, wrong street, and nothing in the service’s own fields says so.

DBI::dbDisconnect(con)

Where the measurements live
